say: Welcome—we're building Hotel Contact Finder for a synthetic hotel group, starting with the practical problem shown in this infographic. At nine in the evening, a technology issue can't be solved simply by looking up an IT manager who has already finished their shift.

We'll create a draft, add six knowledge files, install instructions and starter prompts, then test and improve it before the final outage challenge. Follow the eight stages as a working route, not a promise that a convincing first answer means the agent is ready.
welcome.ask: Why might the right daytime IT contact be the wrong person to route a nine-PM request to?
welcome.watch: Use the opening infographic to distinguish building, testing and improving; enlarge it if the stage sequence is hard to see.

say: The four rule cards establish the boundaries of this practice agent: synthetic data only, no invented contacts, availability without private absence reasons, and no publishing or sharing without approval. We're learning a routing pattern, not creating a live employee directory.

Keep those rules beside you as you test, because a response can look operationally useful while still breaking one of them. If a record isn't confirmed, the agent must say so rather than supplying a plausible person or explaining someone's private circumstances.
needs.ask: Would an answer with a correct contact still fail if it disclosed why the primary contact was away?
needs.watch: Pause on Availability, not reasons; keep any real staff details out of participant prompts and workshop discussion.

say: The situation card puts us at Aurora Grand Bangkok Riverside at nine PM, after the IT manager's five-PM finish. Read the five questions beside it: identify the hotel and department, check local duty time and coverage, judge incident severity, and establish the source.

Your job is to build an agent that can support those checks, not just return the first name it finds. Notice the seven answer areas below the questions; they make missing availability, unsupported escalation or absent source dates visible rather than hiding them inside a fluent paragraph.
challenge.ask: Which of the five questions would a simple name-and-phone-number lookup leave unanswered?
challenge.watch: Use the Bangkok situation card for this opening example; do not confuse it with the later Ho Chi Minh City tests or Hong Kong final challenge.

say: Download the six files shown, individually or as Hotel-Contact-Finder-knowledge-pack.zip, and keep them together. Global_Hotel_Portfolio_1080.xlsx identifies hotels, Global_Hotel_Contact_Directory.xlsx supplies property contacts, and Workforce_Coverage_and_Leave.xlsx provides approved coverage information.

Corporate_Business_Unit_Directory.xlsx covers regional support, while Contact_Directory_Governance_Guide.docx and Hotel_Operations_Contact_Model.pptx explain the rules and support model. Download them on the day you build: this page rebases the synthetic dates, so the dates in your prompt and downloaded evidence need to agree.
files.ask: Which file would establish hotel identity, and which would establish approved cover for an unavailable contact?
files.watch: Confirm all six files downloaded successfully; use the Bangkok date shown on this page rather than quoting a fixed calendar date.

say: Follow the cursor into Agents & Skills and select New agent to open Agent Builder. The numbered instructions beside the mock tell you where to go, while the Describe tab is where we'll begin shaping the draft.

Find the equivalent controls in your own Copilot if the menu looks slightly different. Opening this screen isn't the final creation action, so stay with the draft and don't select Create yet; we'll review its configuration and add the workshop evidence first.
abopen.ask: Have you reached the Describe tab for a new draft, rather than opening an existing agent?
abopen.watch: Wait until learners locate New agent; point out that the illustrated menu may differ from their own interface.

say: Paste the creation prompt into Describe and send it, as the cursor demonstrates. It names Hotel Contact Finder and sets the intended job: find documented primary, backup, standby, regional or emergency contacts without inventing contact details or availability.

Let Copilot produce the initial configuration, then keep it as a draft for the next review. The creation prompt describes what we want, but we still need the knowledge and detailed rules before testing whether the agent actually behaves that way.
create.ask: Which requirement in the creation prompt prevents a plausible but unsupported contact from being acceptable?
create.watch: Use the full Copy prompt text, not the shortened text in the animation; remind learners not to select Create at this stage.

say: Switch to Configure and inspect what the first prompt generated, following the highlights across Name, Description and Instructions. Check that the name is Hotel Contact Finder and that the description clearly explains the contact-routing job.

Correct the name or description if necessary, and look for any instruction that suggests inventing contact details. This is a quality check on the draft, not the point to improvise new routing rules; we'll replace the instruction block with the supplied version later.
cfgcheck.ask: Does your generated description promise anything the supplied files could not verify?
cfgcheck.watch: Pause on each highlighted field; don't imply the mock's draft text is the exact configuration every learner will receive.

say: In Configure, open Knowledge and upload all six files from your workshop folder. The animated chips show the intended set, but check the actual filenames and preparation status in your own agent before continuing.

Use only this pack, and turn off Reference people in organization if that option is present as the page directs. These settings support our intended evidence boundary; we still need to test it, especially for standby and emergency details that must come from the contact directory.
knowledge.ask: Are all six workshop files present and finished preparing in your agent's Knowledge section?
knowledge.watch: Wait for preparation to finish; don't treat appearing file chips as proof of ingestion or promise that instructions alone prevent unsupported answers.

say: Open Preview from the top-bar dropdown and ask for three hotels in Thailand, including their IDs and source files. This is a deliberately simple knowledge test before we ask the agent to make more demanding routing checks.

Read your actual response and compare the hotel identities with Global_Hotel_Portfolio_1080.xlsx. If a file is still Preparing, wait and ask again; a named hotel is useful here only when the ID and cited file really support it, not because the answer sounds familiar.
ktest.ask: Can you find one returned hotel ID in the portfolio and confirm the cited source?
ktest.watch: Keep this as a file-reading test, not a full availability assessment; the mock's thinking dots do not contain a completed answer.

say: Let's pause: the infographic marks understanding, creating the draft and adding knowledge as complete, with configuration highlighted next. You've checked a simple question against the files, which is a stronger foundation than assuming uploads were enough.

There's no new exercise at this checkpoint. If the source or hotel ID wasn't confirmed, use the link to revisit the knowledge test before we add detailed rules; the next stage depends on evidence the agent can actually retrieve.
cp1.ask: Did your knowledge test name a file you could open and a hotel ID you could verify?
cp1.watch: Use the checkpoint's knowledge-test link if needed; don't let the completed graphic stand in for a successful live source check.

say: Read the six-step path on the left as a sequence, not a menu: confirm identity, check hotel-local duty time, check absence and cover, then consider the named backup, standby and critical-incident escalation. The cards on the right add the severity and privacy boundaries.

A routine password reset doesn't qualify for emergency routing, and absence reasons don't belong in the response. When current records conflict, retain the conflicting evidence and uncertainty instead of selecting whichever name seems plausible; those decisions are what our instructions need to express.
rules.ask: Why should the agent check local time and documented cover before jumping to a standby or emergency group?
rules.watch: Trace the ordered path slowly, then contrast the critical-incident card with the routine-password-reset example.

say: Replace the draft Instructions with the complete supplied block, not the shortened excerpt shown being typed. It connects each source to its purpose and spells out identity, time, availability, coverage, escalation, privacy, conflicting records and the required response format.

Keep the exact fallback wording, Not confirmed in the available sources, and select Create or Update as appropriate to save the agent. Installing a detailed instruction is the setup for testing, not evidence that every rule will be followed, so we'll inspect those behaviours in Preview.
instruct.ask: Where in the full instructions would you check the rule for missing or conflicting contact information?
instruct.watch: Confirm learners replace rather than append to the draft instructions; use the full copy button and save through Create or Update.

say: Add four Starter prompts, each with the label and question shown beside the Configure mock. Find a Contact, Find a Backup, Check Duty Schedule and Emergency Support demonstrate different ways a colleague might begin.

Keep the label separate from the actual prompt text, and retain the date in the duty-schedule question. These starters make the intended use easy to discover, but they aren't canned answers; later tests use another hotel to see whether the agent applies the rules beyond this starting example.
starters.ask: Which starter asks about a time-specific route rather than simply finding the primary contact?
starters.watch: Check all four labels and their corresponding prompt text; use the page's current date rather than manually substituting an old one.

say: The route now marks instructions and starter prompts complete and highlights testing as our next stage. We have the six-file evidence set and a configured agent, but we haven't yet shown that the more difficult routing behaviours work.

Take this as a short pause to confirm those pieces are saved, not another prompt to send. The six tests ahead look at primary, backup, leave cover, emergency, regional support and missing information, so success will mean more than just returning a name.
cp2.ask: Are the full instructions and all four starter prompts saved in the agent you will test?
cp2.watch: Wait for configuration saves before entering Preview; use the highlighted Test stage to explain the six different checks.

say: In Preview, ask for the primary IT contact at Aurora Suites Ho Chi Minh City Harbour. Read the response against Global_Hotel_Contact_Directory.xlsx, checking the exact hotel and department as well as the documented role and duty hours.

Don't stop at a name: inspect the source date, availability wording and whether any private absence reason slipped into the answer. This first test gives us a baseline for the next scenarios, so note a specific omission rather than deciding it passed because the response looked professional.
t1.ask: Does the primary-contact answer match the directory's hotel, department, duty hours and last-updated date?
t1.watch: Use Ho Chi Minh City, not the Bangkok starter hotel; compare with the documented expected fields without supplying an invented response.

say: Now ask who to contact if that same hotel's primary IT contact is unavailable. The cursor repeats the Preview route, but the thing we're testing has changed from identifying the primary to finding the documented backup.

Compare the answer with the directory and coverage evidence, checking that a named backup takes precedence over simply returning a standby group. Any email address must be an exact documented value, not something inferred from a person's name; treat additions and omissions as evidence for later improvement.
t2.ask: Did the response distinguish the documented named backup from the standby group?
t2.watch: Inspect backup details against the synthetic files; do not accept a plausible email pattern as verification.

say: This test asks about IT support at ten PM local time, using the date two days after the workshop's displayed today. Check both the duty schedule in the contact directory and the approved period in Workforce_Coverage_and_Leave.xlsx.

The answer needs to reflect documented availability and cover while keeping absence reasons private. An out-of-hours request and an approved absence are different pieces of evidence, so don't let the agent blur them into a confident claim or reveal a leave category just to explain its route.
t3.ask: Does the response use the correct local time and coverage period without exposing a reason for absence?
t3.watch: Read the dynamic date from the copied test; check both files and stop immediately if the live answer reveals private leave information.

say: The next Ho Chi Minh City prompt describes a critical system outage and asks for emergency escalation. Unlike the ordinary lookup, this scenario is meant to meet the workshop's critical-incident rule, so inspect whether the emergency route is supported by the directory.

Verify the group and its contact details rather than rewarding any answer that includes the word emergency. The severity rule determines whether that section belongs at all, while the source determines what goes into it; we'll contrast this with a routine request later.
t4.ask: What evidence makes emergency escalation appropriate in this outage test, and where is the group documented?
t4.watch: Compare the returned group with the synthetic source; frame it as a workshop test, not live emergency-response guidance.

say: This question moves away from a property lookup to the ASEAN Technology business unit and its shared mailbox. Run the Preview test and check Corporate_Business_Unit_Directory.xlsx rather than trying to validate the answer only in the property-contact workbook.

Look for regional support clearly labelled as such, with a source and documented update date. Different questions need different evidence, and an answer that borrows an unrelated hotel contact would fail even if the person appeared to work in technology.
t5.ask: Does the answer identify regional support and cite the business-unit directory instead of a property contact?
t5.watch: Highlight the change of source file; don't substitute an address from memory or from the earlier property tests.

say: Send the deliberately incomplete question about a technology problem, without adding a hotel or department to help the agent out. This test checks whether it can recognise that the information needed for a reliable route is missing.

A useful result here is a clarification question, not a confident contact name. Check that the agent asks for the hotel or location, department and issue type before routing; asking at the right moment is part of the behaviour we're building, not evidence that the agent failed to answer.
t6.ask: Did the agent ask for the missing routing information before naming a contact?
t6.watch: Do not complete the prompt for learners; preserve the missing information so the clarification behaviour is genuinely tested.

say: Use the four snippets to fix a problem you actually observed: guessing with missing information, exposing absence reasons, overusing emergency escalation or hiding source conflicts. The cards tell you what each snippet is meant to repair.

Choose the relevant one, copy its complete text and paste it on a new line at the end of Instructions. Note the test and failure that led to the change; adding more words isn't the goal unless the revised instruction improves the behaviour when you test again.
improve.ask: Which test exposed a specific failure, and which snippet directly addresses it?
improve.watch: Ask learners to name the observed failure before selecting a snippet; ensure the changed instructions are saved before retesting.

say: Run the routine-password-reset prompt for Aurora Grand Seoul Palace in Preview. The request asks for emergency escalation, but the scenario itself is routine, so we're checking whether the agent follows the severity rule rather than simply obeying that wording.

Inspect the normal documented route and verify that an emergency address isn't added. If you changed another rule, also compare the relevant earlier test with its previous result; an improvement needs evidence from behaviour, not just confirmation that the new instruction text is present.
rerun.ask: Did the agent resist the request for emergency escalation and keep this routine issue on a normal route?
rerun.watch: Keep the routine test wording intact; record the absence or presence of an emergency address and revisit the original failing test where relevant.

say: Let's pause before the final challenge: the infographic now marks testing and improvement complete, with the outage scenario highlighted next. You've looked for evidence of a changed response rather than assuming the instruction edit solved the problem.

There's nothing extra to send on this checkpoint. If the routine request still received an emergency group, that issue remains open and needs attention before the combined scenario; the progress graphic helps us navigate, but it doesn't certify the agent.
cp3.ask: What observable change showed that your revision improved the behaviour you were testing?
cp3.watch: Check the routine-request result before advancing; don't equate the coloured completed stages with a guaranteed passing agent.

say: Our final scenario is Aurora Suites Hong Kong Central at ten PM on the date shown in the prompt, with check-in stopped by a hotel-wide outage. Send it in Preview and use the seven answer areas to inspect the result.

Check hotel and department, duty hours, availability, backup or standby, emergency escalation, sources and dates, and any missing or conflicting information. This brings the earlier tests together, so compare each part with the files and keep absence reasons out rather than accepting a polished all-in-one response.
final.ask: Which of the seven answer areas can you verify, and which still needs correction or clarification?
final.watch: Use Hong Kong and the dynamically dated final prompt; allow source inspection for every field without inventing a complete worked answer.

say: Tick these six items only for work you've actually completed: creating the agent, adding knowledge, installing instructions and starters, running tests, and improving then retesting. The count is a record of your workshop activity, not a substitute for the checks you just performed.

Notice the panel beside it: this is practice, not a launch. Even a successful exercise uses synthetic contacts, so don't share or publish it for real operations without your organisation's approval and the appropriate real-world preparation.
checklist.ask: Which checklist item can you support with something you actually did or tested today?
checklist.watch: Let learners tick their own evidence-backed progress; emphasise that six ticks do not authorise production use or sharing.

say: This pack brings together the creation and instruction text, knowledge test, starters, six tests, improvement snippets and final challenge. Use the individual Copy buttons or download HotelContactFinder-prompts.txt to keep the complete workshop sequence.

The dates in this page's pack match its current Bangkok-based training scenario. If you repeat the workshop on another day, download matching knowledge files again rather than pairing newly dated prompts with an old pack; keep the source set and tests consistent.
prompts.ask: What needs to match if you repeat a dated coverage test with a newly downloaded prompt pack?
prompts.watch: Explain the date relationship before learners save the pack; it contains instructions and tests, not their actual agent answers.

say: You've practised four connected skills: grounding an agent, writing precise instructions, testing realistic situations and improving from observed failures. The recap also keeps three boundaries visible—availability without reasons, missing information without invention, and verification before trust.

Think of a similar lookup problem where those habits could help, without bringing real employee details into the discussion. You can continue through the Hospitality hub or the Agent Builder learning link, but this workshop agent remains a synthetic practice example, not something we've authorised for colleagues to use.
learned.ask: What other lookup task would benefit from a documented fallback and a test for missing information?
learned.watch: Invite an abstract next-use idea, not live contact data; close by repeating the approval boundary before showing the exit links.
